reading.synopsis: In a Free Union government dependent on telepathic mutants ('teeps') born from a nuclear accident to police ideological loyalty, mysterious metal 'hoods' begin circulating that block mind-probes entirely, and anyone caught wearing one is mobbed and stripped of it by a suspicious public egged on by teep agents. Government official Walter Franklin receives a hood anonymously, wears it out of simple curiosity about mental privacy, and is instantly framed as disloyal by teeps who had already secretly probed and condemned him before the hood ever reached him. Rescued and brought to the underground 'Hood Maker' organization led by James Cutter, Franklin learns the teeps are engineering a total takeover of government through a pending Anti-Immunity Bill that would criminalize hood-wearing entirely. Sent with Cutter to persuade a key senator to oppose the bill, Franklin is casually murdered the moment they arrive by teep agent Ernest Abbud, who has infiltrated the senator's estate — but Cutter, forced to remove his own hood and be scanned, reveals in the story's final twist that the teeps are not true mutants at all but a sterile genetic accident incapable of reproduction, meaning their entire claimed evolutionary destiny to rule humanity is a lie that will die out with them regardless of who wins the political struggle.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the hood phenomenon and Franklin's frame-up, his rescue and introduction to the resistance, and a final confrontation revealing the teeps' hidden biological vulnerability
movements: Walter Franklin, an ordinary government official, receives an anonymous hood, wears it out of curiosity, and is instantly mobbed and framed as disloyal by teep operatives who had already condemned him before he ever put it on.

Rescued by an underground resistance, Franklin learns hood-maker James Cutter's organization exists to protect prominent officials from teep frame-ups, and that a pending Anti-Immunity Bill threatens to criminalize the hoods that are their only defense.

Franklin is casually murdered attempting to reach a key senator, but Cutter, cornered and forced to remove his own hood, reveals that the teeps are not evolutionary successors to humanity at all but a sterile genetic accident who will die out regardless of the political outcome.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Clearance officials, Franklin's desperate flight, and finally Cutter's calculated confrontation, so the reader assembles the full scope of the teep conspiracy gradually, alongside Franklin's own dawning understanding.
structure.central_device: A political thriller about surveillance and resistance whose actual resolution is biological rather than political -- the teeps' claimed destiny as humanity's evolutionary successors, used to justify their assumption of total power, is revealed to be a self-serving myth contradicted by their simple, verifiable sterility, undercutting the entire ideological basis for their seizure of control regardless of any single battle's outcome.

characters.name: Walter Franklin
characters.note: His mild, curious decision to wear an anonymously-sent hood -- 'if he wore the hood his mind would be his own' -- is the story's sympathetic, ordinary-scale entry point into a much larger conspiracy, and his casual murder partway through denies the story any conventional single-hero resolution.

characters.name: James Cutter
characters.note: His calm willingness to be scanned in the story's final confrontation, and his prepared revelation of the teeps' sterility, reframes what looked like a losing tactical battle into confirmation that the teeps' larger strategic war was unwinnable from the start.

characters.name: Ernest Abbud
characters.note: His casual murder of the unarmed, elderly Franklin ('he was an old man... he wouldn't have lasted long') and his subsequent horrified suicide upon learning his own group's sterility together dramatize both the teeps' ruthlessness and the fragility of the ideological certainty underlying it.

characters.name: Director Ross and Peters
characters.note: Their uneasy, half-suppressed discomfort at the teeps' increasing autonomy and overreach (running an unauthorized total probe on Franklin without permission) shows the human government apparatus is itself already losing control of the mutant faction it created to serve it.

settings.name: New York City under Clearance surveillance
settings.note: An ordinary urban setting transformed by mob violence and loyalty hysteria, in which strangers on the street readily attack and strip a man of his hood on nothing more than a shouted accusation.

settings.name: The Hood Maker's warehouse factory
settings.note: A makeshift underground manufacturing operation staffed by framed refugees, its improvised, unglamorous physical reality contrasting with the outsized political stakes of what it produces.

settings.name: Senator Waldo's guarded estate
settings.note: Revealed to already be compromised -- Waldo himself is a teep -- confirming that the resistance's entire strategic plan was doomed before Franklin and Cutter ever arrived.

motifs: A mob readily turning on an individual accused of concealment, treating the mere desire for mental privacy as self-evident proof of guilt
A ruling or aspiring class's claimed evolutionary or biological destiny used to justify political domination, later revealed to be false or fatally incomplete
Government institutions gradually losing control over a faction they created and empowered to serve their own security needs
A resistance movement's tactical loss (Franklin's death, the infiltrated senator) recontextualized by a deeper strategic revelation that changes the terms of the entire conflict
reading.significance: The story's real twist is not political but biological: the teeps' claim to be homo superior, naturally destined to lead a species they consider genuinely inferior, is punctured not by defeating them in political combat but by the simple demographic fact that not one teep child has ever been born. This reframes the entire preceding thriller plot -- mob violence, government surveillance, assassination, infiltrated senators -- as a battle over control of a present that the losing side (the teeps) has no biological future in regardless of its outcome. The story's closing irony belongs to Abbud, who learns his own group's fatal secret by scanning the very mind that was supposed to be his victim, and chooses suicide rather than live with the knowledge that his claimed destiny was always a dead end.
reading.closing_note: Cutter's own weary, ironic invitation -- 'Scan me. I have nothing to hide. Get a teep in here for a probe -- if you can find any' -- closes the story with the teeps' collapse implied rather than shown, their downfall already guaranteed by biology rather than by anything the surviving human characters have yet managed to accomplish.

distinctive_terms.label: Bill
distinctive_terms.note: The pending Anti-Immunity Bill is the story's central political stake, its progress tracked throughout as the resistance's central obstacle.

distinctive_terms.label: Girl
distinctive_terms.note: The unnamed young resistance driver who rescues Franklin from the mob and Clearance cars.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a ruling mutant faction's claimed status as humanity's evolutionary successors, revealed to be a fatal genetic dead end (total sterility) rather than a genuine biological advance
a telepathic surveillance class using loyalty accusations and mob violence to seize political control from the ordinary government apparatus that created and empowered them

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on his choice to resolve the story's political conflict through a biological revelation rather than a direct confrontation or victory?
Is this story ever discussed alongside Dick's other telepath/mutant stories as part of a broader skepticism toward claims of evolutionary or biological destiny justifying political power?
What becomes of the resistance and the Anti-Immunity Bill after the story's end, now that the teeps' sterility is known to at least one surviving hood-maker? The text leaves this entirely open.
